terms.grammar: conjunction, with the subjunctive; the main clause often has autem or tamen
evidence: Cic. Sen. 17: cum aliī mālōs scandant, … ille autem clāvum tenēns quiētus sedeat in puppī
terms.comment: Adversative cum: the clause states the fact the main clause is set against. Often Latin needs no conjunction at all: it puts the two clauses side by side and sets their first words against each other (illī … hī), with at or autem in the second.

terms.gloss: whereas, but on the other hand
terms.grammar: conjunctions; autem after the first word
evidence: Liv. 1.7.1: tempore illī praeceptō, at hī numerō avium rēgnum trahēbant
Gell. 13.24.2: vitiō vertunt, quia multa egeō; at ego illīs, quia nequeunt egēre
terms.comment: The English “whereas” clause becomes a main clause with the contrasting word first.

terms.gloss: on the other hand, on the contrary
terms.comment: Sets a contrary statement against the last: sunt autem aliī philosophī quī contrā … (Plaut., Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: cum aliī mālōs scandant, aliī per forōs cursent, aliī sentīnam exhauriant, ille autem clāvum tenēns quiētus sedeat in puppī
phrases.english: while some climb the masts, others run along the gangways and others bail out the bilge, he sits quietly in the stern holding the tiller

phrases.latin: tempore illī praeceptō, at hī numerō avium rēgnum trahēbant
phrases.english: the one side claimed the kingdom by being first, whereas the other claimed it by the number of birds

phrases.latin: vitiō vertunt, quia multa egeō; at ego illīs, quia nequeunt egēre
phrases.english: they find fault with me because I go without many things, whereas I find fault with them because they cannot go without
